757.title: "If he said it, it is true"
757.hook: Mecca mocks the night journey, and Abu Bakr says, if he said it, it is true (sirah)
757.carry: he weighed the speaker, not the distance
757.howItsDone: Muslims remember Abu Bakr by the title al-Siddiq and retell his answer when they recall the night journey, often on the night of al-Isra wal-Mi'raj.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Musa, and fifty become five. Your line was: five, weighing fifty. Did one of the prayers land differently, knowing what it weighs? Day seven hundred fifty-seven.

Morning in Mecca. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells the people what happened in the night: he was carried to Jerusalem and brought back before dawn. In the sirah the reaction is fast. Some laugh. Ibn Ishaq reports that some who had believed turned back. A caravan, people say, takes a month to get there and a month to return, and he did it in one night? A few of them hurry off to find his close friend, Abu Bakr. Have you heard what your companion is saying now? Today: al-Siddiq.
screen: `CARRIED BY NIGHT.` → `MECCA LAUGHS.` → `THEY RUN TO ABU BAKR.`

segments.voice: Abu Bakr listens to them. Then he asks one question first: did he say that? Yes, they say. In Ibn Ishaq's account he answers: if he said it, then it is true. And he adds something like this. Why are you so surprised? He tells me news comes to him from heaven, from God, in an hour of the night or the day, and I believe him in that. This is further than Jerusalem. Then Abu Bakr goes to the Prophet, and asks him to describe the city, and as he describes it, Abu Bakr keeps saying: you have spoken the truth. Tradition says this is the day he was called al-Siddiq, the one who affirms the truth. Bukhari has a report from the Prophet's side of that morning too: when Quraysh would not believe him, Allah showed him Jerusalem, and he described it to them while looking at it. Notice what Abu Bakr's trust rests on. It isn't a feeling about miracles. It's long knowledge of one man, and of what he has said before. So Abu Bakr doesn't weigh the distance to Jerusalem. He weighs the speaker. And with his answer, this part of the story, the part of sorrow, Ta'if and the night journey, comes to its close. It began with two graves, Khadijah's and Abu Talib's. It closes with a friend who stays when others mock.
screen: `DID HE SAY THAT?` · `IF HE SAID IT, IT IS TRUE.` · `HE WEIGHS THE SPEAKER.` · `AL-SIDDIQ: THE ONE WHO AFFIRMS.` · then, large: `IF HE SAID IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: trust someone you know to be honest. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one person whose word has held, again and again. Someone who said they'd come, and came. Someone who told you the hard thing when the easy thing was right there. Let their face settle in front of you. Now notice how much of your life rests on people like this, quietly. Is there something they've told you lately that you set aside, or half believed? Hold it again, as if it came from them, because it did. If you pray, you can thank God for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Al-Siddiq, the one who affirms the truth. Abu Bakr's title, earned when he trusted the Prophet's word about the night journey without arguing the distance. Today's word.
Your line: he weighed the speaker, not the distance. Today, tell one honest person in your life that their word counts with you, and say why. Day seven hundred fifty-seven.

758.title: Six men from Yathrib
758.hook: at the pilgrimage six men from Yathrib listen and believe
758.howItsDone: Muslims retell the meeting with the six men of Yathrib as the start of the road to Medina, the turning point after the hardest years in Mecca.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Bakr's answer. Your line was: he weighed the speaker, not the distance. Whose word did you lean on yesterday? Day seven hundred fifty-eight.
screen: `HE WEIGHED THE SPEAKER, NOT THE DISTANCE.`

segments.voice: Pilgrimage season. Tents and travelers fill the valleys around Mecca, and tribes come from far away. Ibn Ishaq says the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, made a habit of these crowds: he would go from camp to camp, introduce himself, and ask who would hear him out. Mostly they turned away. After Ta'if, after the mocking, he keeps going. Then one evening, near a place called Aqaba, he meets a small group from a town to the north. Ibn Ishaq counts them: six men from Yathrib. He asks them a simple question. Will you sit with me, and let me speak to you? Today: Yathrib.
screen: `CAMP AFTER CAMP.` → `MOSTLY TURNED AWAY.` → `WILL YOU SIT WITH ME?`

segments.voice: They sit. He tells them about God, and recites the Qur'an to them. And here, Ibn Ishaq says, something had already prepared them. In Yathrib they lived beside Jewish neighbors who were people of scripture, and those neighbors had spoken of a prophet who would come. So the six look at each other and say: this may be the prophet they told us about. Let's not be the last to answer him. And they believe. Notice what they bring with them. Yathrib was a town worn down by feuding between its own clans. The six tell him so: we have left our people, and no people are so divided by enmity as they are. Perhaps God will unite them through you. We'll go home and call them to this, and if God gathers them around you, no man will be stronger than you. Then they go home, and they talk. Ibn Ishaq says that before long there was hardly a house in Yathrib where the Prophet wasn't being spoken of. Look at the shape of this. Years of closed doors in Mecca. A walk to Ta'if that ended in stones. And then six strangers, from a town he has never lived in, who simply listen. Nobody in the story argues them into it. They sit, they hear, and they take what they heard home. This begins a new part of the story: toward Yathrib, the town that will one day be called Medina, the city.
screen: `THEY SIT, AND HE RECITES.` · `THIS MAY BE THE PROPHET.` · `A TOWN WORN DOWN BY FEUDS.` · `THEY TAKE IT HOME.` · then, large: `SIX LISTENED.`

segments.voice: The practice: listen to a stranger kindly. Sit, and breathe slowly for a moment. Now think of the strangers who cross your day: someone at a counter, a new person at work, a neighbor you've only nodded to, a voice on a customer service line. Pick one you'll likely meet soon. Picture actually sitting with them, or standing, and letting them finish. Not planning your reply. Not checking the time. Just hearing what they have to say. Notice how rare that is, and how cheap. If you pray, you can ask God for an open ear today. The bell holds the time.
Yathrib. The town, later called Medina, whose six strangers sat, listened to the Prophet at the pilgrimage, believed, and carried the news home. Today's word.
Your line: six listened. Today, give one stranger your whole attention until they finish speaking, without planning what you'll say next. Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

759.title: The first pledge of Aqaba
759.hook: twelve pledge not to steal, lie, kill their children or slander
759.howItsDone: Muslims remember the first pledge of Aqaba as a promise about how to live, and the same list of conduct appears in the Qur'an's description of women pledging to the Prophet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yathrib. Your line was: six listened. Did a stranger get your full attention, even for a minute? Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

A year goes by. The pilgrimage comes round again, and so do the men from Yathrib. This time, Ibn Ishaq says, there are twelve of them. They meet the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at the same spot, Aqaba, a narrow pass on the edge of Mina, away from the crowds. They've had a year at home to talk, to argue, to wonder. Now they've come back with their hands out. Not to ask for anything. To give their word. Today: the first pledge of Aqaba.
screen: `A YEAR LATER.` → `TWELVE COME BACK.` → `HANDS OUT TO PLEDGE.`

segments.voice: What did they promise? Ubada ibn al-Samit, whom the sirah names among the twelve, gives the terms in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet said: pledge to me that you will not set up any partner with God, that you will not steal, that you will not commit adultery, that you will not kill your children, that you will not bring a slander you have invented between your hands and feet, and that you will not disobey me in what is right. Whoever keeps it, his reward is with God. Look at that list. There's no army in it. No money. No promise to fight for anyone. It's almost entirely about how they will live. Their hands, their tongues, their homes, their children. Ibn Ishaq says this kind of pledge came to be called the pledge of women, and that it carried no promise of war. The Qur'an, in surah sixty, describes believing women pledging much the same things to the Prophet. And there's a mercy built in. In Ubada's report the Prophet adds: whoever falls into any of these and is punished in this world, that is an expiation. And whoever falls and God covers it, it is up to God, to forgive or to punish. So the pledge is clear, and it's also realistic. It expects people to be tested. It doesn't throw them away when they stumble. These twelve go home carrying a promise about conduct. Not yet a promise of protection. That comes later.
screen: `NO PARTNER WITH GOD.` · `NO STEALING, NO SLANDER.` · `NO ARMY, NO MONEY.` · `ROOM FOR THOSE WHO STUMBLE.` · then, large: `A PLEDGE OF CONDUCT.`

segments.voice: The practice: make one clear promise. Settle, and breathe. The twelve didn't promise to be good in general. They named things. So name one. Look over the list from the story: don't take what isn't yours, don't say what isn't true about someone, guard the people in your house. Or find your own. One behavior you know needs a line drawn under it. Say it to yourself in a single plain sentence, the kind you could actually keep. Not forever. Just clearly. Then sit with it. Notice whether it feels heavy, or light, or both. If you pray, you can place it before God. The bell holds the time.
Aqaba, the narrow pass where twelve men of Yathrib pledged the Prophet a way of living, not a war. Today's word.
Your line: a pledge of conduct. Today, keep the one plain promise you made in the sit, and notice the moment it gets tested. Day seven hundred fifty-nine.

760.title: Mus'ab the teacher
760.hook: Mus'ab ibn Umayr is sent to teach the Qur'an in Yathrib, and many believe
760.howItsDone: Muslims remember Mus'ab ibn Umayr as the teacher sent to Yathrib before the hijra, and his invitation to sit and listen is often retold when people talk about how to share the faith gently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pledge at Aqaba. Your line was: a pledge of conduct. Did your one plain promise get tested? Day seven hundred sixty.

The twelve are heading home with a promise and a problem. They believe, but who will teach them? Who will recite the Qur'an to their families, lead their prayer, answer the questions that come up at dinner? So the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, sends someone with them. Not a clan elder. Mus'ab ibn Umayr, a Meccan who, tradition says, had left a comfortable life behind for this faith. Ibn Ishaq says that in Yathrib people came to call him simply the reciter. Today: al-Muqri.
screen: `WHO WILL TEACH THEM?` → `MUS'AB IS SENT.` → `THEY CALL HIM THE RECITER.`

segments.voice: Mus'ab stays with a man of Yathrib, As'ad ibn Zurara, and the two of them go out into the gardens and neighborhoods, reciting. Not everyone is pleased. Ibn Ishaq tells of one day when a clan leader, Usayd ibn Hudayr, comes striding toward them with his spear, angry. What have you come here for, to make fools of our weak ones? Leave us, if you value your life. And Mus'ab doesn't argue. He says, roughly: will you not sit down and listen? If you like what you hear, accept it. If you dislike it, we'll keep away from what you dislike. Usayd thinks that's fair. He plants his spear in the ground and sits. Mus'ab recites. And the story says that before Usayd had spoken a word, they could see the change in his face. He asks what a person does to enter this faith. Then Usayd goes and sends a greater leader, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, who comes in just as angry, and the same thing happens: an invitation to sit, a recitation, a changed face. Ibn Ishaq says Sa'd then went back to his own clan and asked how they regarded him, and when they answered with respect, he told them he would not speak to them until they believed. And tradition says that by evening, his clan had. Here's what Mus'ab's teaching looks like. Sit down. Listen. You are free to say no. That's the whole method in the story. The teacher's job is to put the words in front of people, and step back.
screen: `A SPEAR AND A THREAT.` · `WILL YOU NOT SIT AND LISTEN?` · `IF YOU DISLIKE IT, WE STOP.` · `A CHANGED FACE.` · then, large: `THE FIRST TEACHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: teach one verse to someone. Sit, and breathe. Choose a short line you know, one you could say without a page in front of you. If you're Muslim, it might be a line from a short surah. In Pickthall's old translation, the hundred and twelfth surah opens: Say: He is Allah, the One! If you're not, it can be any line that matters to you. Now think of one person who might like to hear it: a child, a friend, a coworker who asked once. Picture saying it to them, the way Mus'ab did: here it is, take it or leave it. Then say the line once, quietly, to yourself. The bell holds the time.
Al-Muqri, the reciter. Mus'ab ibn Umayr's name in Yathrib, where he recited the Qur'an to anyone who would sit, and left them free to say no. Today's word.
Your line: the first teacher. Today, pass on one line you love to one person, and let them do what they like with it. Day seven hundred sixty.

761.title: The second pledge
761.hook: seventy-three men and two women pledge to protect him as their own
761.howItsDone: Muslims remember the second pledge of Aqaba as the promise that opened the way to Medina, and honor the Ansar, the helpers of Medina, for keeping it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Muqri. Your line was: the first teacher. Did you pass on a line to someone, and leave them free with it? Day seven hundred sixty-one.

Another pilgrimage. Another night at Aqaba. But this time it's after dark, a third of the night gone, and people are slipping away from their sleeping companions one or two at a time, Ibn Ishaq says, creeping like birds. They gather in a ravine. Ibn Ishaq counts them: seventy-three men and two women. One of the women is Nusayba bint Ka'b, known as Umm Umara. They've come to make a different kind of promise than the twelve made a year before. Today: Aqaba.
screen: `AFTER DARK, IN A RAVINE.` → `SLIPPING AWAY ONE BY ONE.` → `SEVENTY-THREE MEN, TWO WOMEN.`

segments.voice: The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, comes with his uncle al-Abbas, who, Ibn Ishaq says, still followed the religion of his people but came to look after his nephew. Al-Abbas speaks first, and he's blunt. He is safe among his own clan. If you're going to take him, be sure you can protect him. If not, leave him now. Then the Prophet recites the Qur'an to them, and asks for their pledge: that they protect him as they protect their own women and children. Al-Bara ibn Ma'rur takes his hand and says yes: we are people of war and weapons. Then another man, Abu al-Haytham, raises a hard question. We have ties with other people in Yathrib, and we'll be cutting them. If we do this, and God gives you victory, will you go back to your own people and leave us? And the story says the Prophet smiled, and answered: no. Blood is blood. I am of you and you are of me. I will fight whom you fight, and make peace with whom you make peace. Look at what's changed from the first pledge. That one was about conduct. This one is about bodies and homes: we will stand in front of you. And it runs both ways. They ask for his loyalty as clearly as he asks for theirs. Their reward, he tells them, is paradise. In the story, no wealth is promised, and no power. Only that.
screen: `AL-ABBAS: PROTECT HIM OR LEAVE HIM.` · `AS YOU PROTECT YOUR OWN.` · `WILL YOU LEAVE US LATER?` · `I AM OF YOU, YOU ARE OF ME.` · then, large: `PROTECT HIM AS YOUR OWN.`

segments.voice: The practice: be someone's protector. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people you already protect without thinking: a child, a parent, a partner, a friend. Now widen it by one. Who in your life is exposed right now, and has nobody standing in front of them? A new kid at school. A coworker who gets talked over. A neighbor living alone. Hold that person for a moment. Then picture one ordinary, concrete thing you could do to cover them this week: walking with them, speaking up, checking in. Keep it small enough to actually do. If you pray, you can ask God to keep them safe. The bell holds the time.
Aqaba. The ravine where, at night, seventy-three men and two women of Yathrib pledged to protect the Prophet as their own families, and he pledged he was theirs. Today's word.
Your line: protect him as your own. Today, do the one small thing that puts you between someone exposed and whatever's coming at them. Day seven hundred sixty-one.

762.title: Slipping out
762.hook: Muslims leave Mecca quietly, in small groups, leaving homes and property
762.howItsDone: Muslims call those who left Mecca for Medina the Muhajirun, the emigrants, and retell stories like Umm Salama's and Suhayb's to honor what the hijra cost them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aqaba. Your line was: protect him as your own. Who did you stand in front of? Day seven hundred sixty-two.

A door closes in Mecca before dawn, and the family behind it isn't coming back. With the pledge made, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells his followers they can go: God has given them brothers in Yathrib and a home to go to. And so they go. Not all together. In ones and twos and families, quietly, so Quraysh won't stop them. Houses are left standing behind them. Today: slipping out.
screen: `A DOOR CLOSES BEFORE DAWN.` → `IN ONES AND TWOS.` → `HOUSES LEFT STANDING.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq keeps some of these departures in close-up. One is Umm Salama's. She sets out with her husband, Abu Salama, and their little son. Her own clan stops them and takes her back: you can go, they tell him, but not with our daughter. Then his clan arrives, furious, and takes the child: if you've kept her, we keep our boy. In a single stop on the road, a family is pulled into three pieces. Abu Salama goes on to Yathrib alone. Umm Salama, in her own telling, goes out every morning to the place where it happened and weeps until evening, for a long time, until a relative takes pity and persuades the clans to let her go. She gets her son back and sets out, alone, on a camel, with the boy in her lap. Another is Suhayb, called the Roman, who had come to Mecca with nothing and done well there in trade. As he leaves, the story goes, men of Quraysh block him: you came here poor and grew rich among us, and now you'll leave with it all? He asks: if I give you my wealth, will you let me pass? They say yes, and he hands it over. When the Prophet hears, tradition says he answered: Suhayb has made a profitable trade. That's what slipping out looked like. Not a march. A long series of private losses, chosen one by one: a house, savings, a morning by the road. The Qur'an speaks of those who emigrated and were driven from their homes and their wealth. These are some of their faces.
screen: `A FAMILY PULLED INTO THREE.` · `WEEPING EACH MORNING.` · `SUHAYB HANDS OVER HIS WEALTH.` · `A PROFITABLE TRADE.` · then, large: `THEY LEFT EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: The practice: leave something behind for good. Sit, and breathe. Nobody is asking you to hand over your savings. Start smaller. Think of one thing you're carrying that you've known for a while you need to put down: a grudge, a habit, a shelf of things you keep for a life you no longer live, a conversation you replay at night. Pick one. Picture setting it down by the road, the way those families left their doors. Not angrily. Just leaving. Notice what it costs, and what you might travel lighter without it. If you pray, you can ask God to help you not turn back for it. The bell holds the time.
Slipping out. The believers left Mecca quietly in small groups, leaving houses, wealth, and sometimes family behind on the road to Yathrib. Today's word.
Your line: they left everything. Today, actually let go of the one thing you named, by giving it away, deleting it, or simply not picking it back up. Day seven hundred sixty-two.

763.title: The plot
763.hook: the Meccan leaders plan to kill him with a man from every clan
763.howItsDone: Muslims recite the verse about this plot (8:30) and retell the night of the council when they remember the hijra, often as a reminder to trust God's planning over their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, slipping out. Your line was: they left everything. Did you set one thing down, and leave it there? Day seven hundred sixty-three.

Mecca is emptying out. House after house of believers stands locked, their owners gone north to Yathrib, where they now have protectors. The leaders of Quraysh can see where this is heading. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is still in the city, with Abu Bakr and Ali. If he joins the others, he'll be out of their reach, among people sworn to defend him. So they call a meeting in the council house, the Dar al-Nadwa. One question on the table: what do we do about him? Today: the plot.
screen: `MECCA EMPTYING OUT.` → `THE COUNCIL HOUSE.` → `WHAT DO WE DO ABOUT HIM?`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq records the debate. One voice says: lock him up in irons and wait for him to die, as poets have died before. No, says another: his followers will hear and come to free him. Another says: drive him out, and we'll be rid of him. No: look how sweet his speech is and how he wins hearts. He'll gather an army and come back. Then Abu Jahl gives the plan they choose. Take one strong young man from every clan, give each a sharp sword, and let them strike him all at once, like a single man. Then his blood will be spread across all the clans, and his family can't fight everyone. They'll have to take blood money instead. It's a cold plan, and clever. It isn't one man's crime. It's everyone's, so it's no one's. Ibn Ishaq adds a strange detail: the voice that knocked down prison and exile, and praised the killing, belonged to an old man from Najd who had joined the meeting, and Ibn Ishaq says he was Iblis, Satan, in disguise. What the Qur'an itself says about that night is short. It reminds the Prophet of when those who disbelieved plotted against him, to hold him captive, or kill him, or drive him out. They plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of planners. In the common reading, the verse lists the same three options the council argued over: captivity, killing, exile. And the verse doesn't describe a counter-army. It just sets their planning beside God's.
screen: `LOCK HIM UP, OR DRIVE HIM OUT?` · `A YOUNG MAN FROM EVERY CLAN.` · `EVERYONE'S CRIME, NO ONE'S.` · `THEY PLOTTED, AND GOD PLOTTED.` · then, large: `THEY PLANNED; ALLAH PLANNED.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray for protection, or, if you don't pray, sit with what you'd want protected. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you're anxious about this week: a decision others are making about you, a meeting, a diagnosis, a person who seems set against you. Let it be as real as it is. Now notice the size of the planning that's out of your hands. Then notice that the story doesn't end with the council's vote. If you pray, you can ask God for protection in your own words, or with a line you already know from the Qur'an. If you don't, simply breathe out the part you can't control. The bell holds the time.
The plot. Quraysh planned to kill the Prophet with a man from every clan, and the Qur'an sets their plotting beside God's. Today's word.
Your line: they planned; Allah planned. Today, when you catch yourself running every possible outcome, stop, and hand one of them over. Day seven hundred sixty-three.

fork.setup: you sit on the council. someone proposes exile: just drive him out. what does the room decide?
options: kill him with a man from every clan.
fork.reveal: they rejected prison and exile, and chose Abu Jahl's plan. the Qur'an answers: they plotted, and God plotted.

original.note: Arabic: plotting, scheming; the word the Qur'an uses for both their plan and God's.

trapdoor: what you thought: some enemies wanted him dead.
what it means: a council designed a killing to be everyone's crime and no one's, and the Qur'an sets God's planning beside theirs.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq's account of Dar al-Nadwa and Abu Jahl's proposal; Qur'an 8:30 names captivity, killing and exile, and uses the same word for both plots.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Quraysh meet in Dar al-Nadwa; proposals to imprison or exile; Abu Jahl's plan of a young man from every clan; the old man of Najd)
